title: Ripple — Supply Chain Distribution Game
description: A supply chain ordering game for classes. A team runs a chain from store to plant on one device, turn by turn behind a hand-over screen so each stage sees only its own numbers (or at an open table), with simulated players for any stage nobody holds; orders and shipments take time to travel, so small changes in customer demand become large swings upstream. The debrief charts the bullwhip and the stock and backlog of every stage, compares the team with the same chain played by typical players and by the best simple rule, reads each player's decision rule from their orders (how much of what was already on order they counted, how fast they corrected, how they forecast), replays the game with every stage counting more of its supply line, and shows time used beside cost. Configurable chain length, delays, costs and four demand patterns; saved after every decision; CSV export.

title: AI Expectations Gap Map
description: A board that replaces the hype-cycle curve with two measurable axes: market expectations and demonstrated value, for 27 AI technologies. The gap between them is the risk, and bubble size is the business impact if the technology delivers. Five scenario drivers (capability progress, capital availability, regulatory pressure, inference cost decline and enterprise data readiness) and six preset scenarios project the board forward with a two-stock model: evidence grows logistically, expectations adjust toward evidence plus a narrative premium. Lists show where a correction is most likely and what is underpriced, each with the signal that would confirm or kill the bet. Starting positions come from analyst scores, from public attention signals collected monthly (Wikipedia page views, Hacker News, arXiv, PyPI downloads), or a blend; a monthly job opens a pull request with the new signals and flags every score they contradict, and a quarterly issue prompts the analyst review. Every technology comes with a plain description and a supply chain example. Each month the board's forecasts are frozen in a ledger that is never rewritten, and a track record scores them as they come due against a forecast that nothing moves. The same job looks for rising AI terms the board does not track yet (Hacker News stories and arXiv papers) and lists them with a Wikipedia description, for the analyst to decide. Any view can be shared as a link.

title: Robot Configurator
description: Describe the robot you want (a wheeled rover, a desktop arm, or a rover carrying an arm) and get designs you can build from parts sold in Denmark, Sweden or Norway. Every compatible combination of chassis, motor, wheel, driver, battery, regulator and controller (or frame, servos and power supply) is checked against motor torque on the slope, tyre grip, top speed, driver and regulator voltage and current, battery discharge, runtime, 3.3 V logic levels, free pins, servo holding torque at the required reach and tipping. The best designs are priced as landed cost, with each parcel's shipping, VAT, IOSS/VOEC or import duty and clearance fees, choosing the vendor mix exactly. Three proposals (lowest cost, most headroom on the cost–headroom frontier, quickest delivery) compare side by side; a chart shows every design by cost and headroom, any point can be picked, and any part swapped to see what it costs and which check stops it. Each design comes with its budget, a step-by-step build guide, power and signal wiring, and two Arduino sketches (a self-test and the robot program with speed control, obstacle avoidance, line following, measured moves, arm inverse kinematics and teach/replay, over USB, Bluetooth or a Wi-Fi phone page) that compile for Uno, Nano and ESP32 with no extra libraries. When nothing fits it says which checks block the closest designs and how far each requirement must move. Every price is either checked on the shop's own product page, with the link and the date, or marked as an estimate, and a weekly job follows every link; designs can be limited to checked prices. A drawing shows the rover from above with every board placed on the chassis (and a second deck when they do not fit) and the power wiring, and the arm from the side with its reach; a build pack puts everything on one page to print or save as PDF. A validation page runs the engine live on cases with a known answer, and a built robot can be measured against the model (the self-test prints the numbers to paste) and the result sent in to calibrate the models. In English, Danish, Swedish, Norwegian and Spanish.

title: Tierwise
description: Multi-tier capacity planning for a food supply chain across latitudes. A final consumption forecast at eight consumption points (Mexico City to Manila) becomes the capacity each site needs, tier by tier: warehouses, packaging CMOs, final dosing CMOs, product manufacturing CMOs and raw ingredient CMOs, with several CMOs per tier and sourcing shares between them. Production lead times, quality release times, warehouse handling, safety stock and transit shift every requirement earlier; yields gross it up; the bill of materials converts packs to sachets to tonnes. Sites run from 52°N to 38°S, so demand and milk seasons run six months apart between hemispheres. The outlook is 36 months in monthly periods and 10 more years in yearly periods, each year keeping its busiest month. Load your own supply chain from CSV, Excel or JSON (with templates, decimal commas and errors by row), rename the tiers for another kind of chain, and share the whole plan as a link. Every site's load is traced exactly to the markets and customers behind it; the capacity to add is sized for a utilisation target and applied in one click; any two plans compare side by side as a heatmap of the change. Within capacity, a linear program solved in the browser by HiGHS plans the whole horizon with no site above its capacity: it builds stock ahead of peaks, re-sources among qualified lanes or any supplier, draws safety stock in a crunch, and reports fill rates, unmet demand and bottlenecks market by market. A Network Studio draws the chain by tier, with production sites, warehouses, consumption points and transport routes told apart: add sites, draw routes, drag them into order, edit them in an inspector, define your own parameters for sites and routes, undo anything, and save the diagram as SVG or PNG. A world map shows and edits the same network on the globe, with zoom, pan and routes along their great circles. Routes and parameters travel in every file. A latitude map, a capacity heatmap of 46 periods, tier, lead-time and forecast views, scenarios, an editor for every site and lane, a five-level tutorial with questions, and the whole app in English, Spanish and Danish. 670 tests.

title: Supply Pulse
description: A system-dynamics simulator of a packaged food and dairy supply chain. Demand steps up, peaks for a season, or the plant stops for weeks, and you watch the delays of the chain turn reasonable decisions into empty shelves, amplification and expired stock. Forecasting, hiring and training people, QA release and shipping each add a delay. Batches are held by QA until their microbiological tests pass (positive release), some are rejected, and the lab can become the bottleneck in a surge; finished stock is aged first-in, first-out, and cases with too little shelf life left for retailers to accept are written off. Optional tiers add a distributor that orders from the plant and a key-ingredient supplier far upstream (milk powder, say) with its own lead time, capacity and outages; the line can be shared in campaigns with cleaning changeovers, and when stock is short an allocation rule decides whether priority customers are served first. The levers are overtime, QA expedited when stock runs low, and the planning policy: target cover, forecast smoothing, correction speed and the weight on the supply line. Each is measured on profit, fill rate, weeks short, bullwhip and waste against a saved baseline that sees the same random demand. The trade-offs are real: overtime ends the shortage after a demand step but makes more stock expire for a short-shelf-life product, and expediting QA pays in an outage only if shortages carry a penalty. A decision lab compares saved scenarios side by side, runs a scenario in 100 demand futures with percentile bands and a head-to-head count against the baseline, ranks which inputs matter most in a tornado, and searches 540 planning policies for the most profitable one that meets a fill-rate target, plotting the trade-off frontier. Ten ready-made scenarios, including premium nutrition, private-label snacks and a holiday peak, import of your own weekly or daily demand, a printable decision report, share links, CSV export, charts with hover read-outs and a table view behind each, a live stock-and-flow diagram and every equation with its value in any week. A play mode puts you in the planner's seat: set the production plan turn by turn, seeing only what a planner sees, then compare your two years with the planning rule on the same demand. A tutorial in three levels (beginner, intermediate, advanced) asks questions whose answers are checked against the model by tests. Fully available in English, Latin American Spanish and Danish, with Danish number formats. The model's tests check exact balance at the start, that every case is accounted for, that a smaller time step gives the same answers, and that the forecast matches its exact solution. 618 passing tests.

title: Clockspeed Balancing
description: A management flight simulator for the conflict between commercial strategy (which moves in months), the product supply chain (about a year) and the network (years). You fly a company for 20 years in quarterly turns. Each quarter you set price, service promise, promotions, launches and markets; inventory cover, flexible capacity and dual sourcing; and capacity to build, close or automate in three regions. Every gap between the three costs money, and it wears down the slow, inertial parts of the company: operational capability (eroded by firefighting), trust between functions, supplier relationships, and customer expectations that ratchet up with every promise and come down slowly. Six weathers, from calm skies to an innovation wave, Eastern growth, a promise war, a storm of disruption and tariffs, and all at once. The cockpit has gauges, fit bars for each level, plain-language advisories, a radar of decisions still in flight, regional detail and 20-year history charts, with undo, autosave and flight files. At landing it compares your flight with holding the starting course, then debriefs it: the flight is replayed with one level moving at a time to show what each clock made or cost alone, what moving them together added, and when each decision actually took effect. A system dynamics model in the tradition of Sterman's flight simulators, with 42 model tests and 19 cockpit tests: a steady state that holds for 20 years, exact accounting, the three clock speeds (about 4, 10 and 33 months), the promise ratchet, an unsupported push against support and pacing, firefighting, complexity creep and resilience.

title: Lag Lab
description: After a demand step, production overshoots and planning calls it forecast error. Lag Lab shows how much really is. A production and workforce model in the style of Sterman's Business Dynamics (ch. 17–19) runs the same step three ways: your plan, the same plan with a perfect forecast, and a perfect forecast with full supply-line accounting and hiring on the capacity gap. It splits the overproduction into the necessary refill of a bigger inventory and pipeline, the structure the delays leave, the share caused by decision rules, and the share that is a forecasting problem. The parts add up exactly and each comes with its remedy; at the defaults only 7% is forecasting. Controls for the step, the production, hiring and training delays, adjustment times, supply-line and vacancy weights, forecast smoothing and the hiring driver; presets, share links, week-by-week charts with hover read-outs, and CSV export. A Model tab draws the model as a stock-and-flow diagram; click any variable for its equation, inputs and values, with the full equation list below, every equation tested against the model's own output. Fully available in English and Latin American Spanish. The model's tests check the delay and smoothing against their exact solutions, exact conservation of material and people, and the textbook results; the decomposition is tested to add up and to vanish when its cause is removed. 86 passing tests.

title: Sensor Deck
description: Every sensor a phone's browser can read, live in one page, with nothing to install. It reads the accelerometer, linear acceleration, gyroscope, compass and orientation, magnetometer, ambient light, location, microphone (level, pitch and spectrum), camera (brightness, colour, torch), multi-touch with pressure, battery, network and screen, plus the phone's model and capabilities. Each card shows the live values, the measured sample rate, a 10-second chart with hover read-outs and a table, and says plainly why a sensor can't be read. Derived readings are worked out from the raw ones: steps and cadence, shakes, a compass needle, a spirit level, the rhythm of the motion (by FFT) and distance walked from good GPS fixes. Recording saves every reading at its own rate as CSV or JSON. A computer view pairs with the phone by QR code and streams the readings directly over WebRTC at about 60 Hz, with a live camera thumbnail, the round-trip time and a button to buzz the phone; every message is checked before use. A demo phone (someone walking in Copenhagen) lets it be tried on any device. For what browsers can't read there is a Sensor Deck Android app (Flutter and Kotlin). It runs the same page and adds the barometer with altitude, battery and air temperature, humidity with dew point, proximity, the hardware step counter, a fingerprint check through Android's BiometricPrompt (Android only ever says whether the print matched), and the raw values of any sensor the phone lists. It was tested on the Android emulator with its virtual sensors. The phone can also stream over a USB cable, with no Wi-Fi or internet in the path. A small Node bridge (no dependencies) runs adb reverse when the phone is plugged in and relays over a local WebSocket. It accepts only the Sensor Deck page and listens on loopback only. 93 passing tests, plus the app's bridge tests.

title: Chess for Kids
description: A chess app for young children, part of the Chess project. Eight worlds teach the pieces one at a time (Rook Road, Bishop Hill, Queen Castle, King Garden, Knight Forest, Pawn Village), then Capture Cave and Checkmate Tower. Each level is a small puzzle: collect stars around rocks, capture sleepy pieces, walk the king to a flag without stepping onto guarded squares, promote a pawn, or find a checkmate in one. Three stars go to finishing in the fewest moves, and that target is proven by a breadth-first search over every level. The checkmate levels are real Lichess puzzles (CC0) with exactly one mating move. Children can then play whole games against three gentle computer opponents: Sleepy Sam, Friendly Fiona and Clever Owl. Sir Hop, a knight mascot, reads every instruction and move aloud. He asks before a piece is left where it can be taken, warns when one is attacked, and suggests a move on request. Stars, trophies and medals reward progress, and big squares suit small fingers on phones and tablets. In English, Spanish, Afrikaans, German, Danish and Dutch. Runs entirely in the browser, with progress kept on the device. 88 passing tests.

title: Plumb
description: A 3D simulator for a two-wheeled balancing robot (v1.3). Real Lagrangian dynamics with wheel slip and a floor the body lands on, integrated with Runge-Kutta, and a cascaded PID controller like real cheap hardware runs. The motors are brushed DC gearmotors built from datasheet numbers: back-EMF sets a real top speed, battery voltage matters, gears have play, and speed comes from quantized wheel encoders. The firmware never sees the true angle: a gyro and accelerometer modelled on the MPU-6050 and LSM6DS33 datasheets feed a choice of tilt estimator (gyro only, accelerometer only, complementary, or a Kalman filter that learns the gyro offset), plotted against the truth. Pick a generic motor or Pololu micro metal gearmotors with their published specs, or the original ideal torque source to compare. Sixteen presets, each shown with a scripted push and checked by a test that it behaves as described: a Balboa-class robot from published Pololu parts, flat battery, sloppy gears, ice, an uncalibrated gyro, accelerometer-only, a too-slow control loop. Tune gains, loop rate, noise and delay live; seeded noise makes runs repeatable. Mass and inertia can also come from a FreeCAD parametric model. 42 passing tests.

title: Xiangqi
description: Xiangqi (Chinese chess) against a friend on one screen, or against the open-source Fairy-Stockfish engine — one of the strongest Xiangqi engines, compiled to WebAssembly and running entirely in your browser — at eight strength levels from beginner to full strength. Full rules: generals confined to the palace and the flying-general rule, hobbled horses, blocked elephants that can't cross the river, cannons that capture over a screen, soldiers that step sideways once across the river, stalemate-loses, and perpetual check adjudicated from threefold repetition. Plus a Classic problems mode: mating problems from 《适情雅趣》 (Shiqing Yaqu, 1570), the oldest surviving Xiangqi problem book, graded by length, and the Four Great Endgames (江湖四大名局) as draw-holding studies against the engine. Every problem was scraped, replayed through the app's own rules and confirmed by Fairy-Stockfish; alternative solutions are judged live by the engine, with hints, a step-through solution viewer and solved-problem tracking. Traditional Chinese-character pieces or Western letters, five board styles, a 3D view you can tilt and turn by dragging, WXF move notation, undo and board flip. The move generator is verified against the published perft counts to depth 4 (3,290,240 positions). A small service worker supplies the cross-origin-isolation headers the multi-threaded engine needs, since GitHub Pages can't.

title: Network Stress Test
description: A supply-network resilience sandbox: build or generate a production/warehouse/consumer network (hundreds of editable nodes) connected by air/sea/road lanes with mode-characteristic defaults, and stress-test it against a real min-cost-flow solver. Phase 1: deterministic disruption scenarios and an N-1 contingency scan (the power-grid idea — which single node or lane, if lost, hurts the most). Phase 2: Monte Carlo random-failure sampling, a Time-to-Survive vs. Time-to-Recover check against consumer inventory buffers, and a greedy adversarial search for the worst combination of simultaneous failures. Every algorithm is unit-tested in Node before touching the UI, and the full pipeline is driven end-to-end in headless Chromium. Multi-file project, no runtime dependencies.

title: Face Morph
description: Live face-landmark detection and triangulated face morphing, entirely on-device. Two small neural nets (TinyFaceDetector + a 68-point landmark CNN, via TensorFlow.js) run in the browser against your camera or an uploaded photo — nothing is ever uploaded, a persistent banner says so. Capture two faces, then morph between them with a real triangulated affine warp and cross-dissolve, the classic technique behind photo-morph effects. The 142-triangle mesh isn't computed live — it's a fixed, offline-verified triangulation (exact area match against the convex hull, so no gaps or overlaps) reused for every pair, since the 68 landmark indices always mean the same point on any detected face. Drag the blend slider, watch it auto-morph, or peek at the triangle mesh itself. Single file, vendored face-api.js, no other dependencies.

title: Warehouse Model
description: An interactive engineering reasoning environment for warehouse design — not a CAD viewer. A real parametric FreeCAD model is the authoritative geometry, and an analytical model shares its layout code (a parity test proves the two agree). Five rack types (selective, double-deep, VNA, push-back, drive-in) with selectivity and practical capacity; flue-space, level-pitch and sprinkler-clearance checks; lift-truck cycle time averaged exactly over every door, aisle, bay and level, with lift time; truck-based receiving and shipping docks sized for the peak hour, with Erlang C truck queues; I-flow or U-flow docks, mid cross-aisles, class-based (ABC) slotting with a demand-skew curve and dual-command trips; fleet size and cost. A discrete-event simulation replays the day — random truck arrivals over an hourly profile, yard queues, lift trucks fetching and storing every pallet — 30 times, showing ranges beside the analytic results, and plays one day back in 3D. Decision support: annual total cost of ownership, saved scenarios side by side, share links, JSON/CSV export, a sensitivity tornado and sweeps, and an optimiser that finds the cheapest designs meeting capacity, selectivity and truck-wait targets. Import real movement and inventory CSVs to set throughput, peaks, inventory and demand skew; export the design as IFC4 (BIM, validated with IfcOpenShell), a DXF floor plan, glTF 3D or the FreeCAD command that regenerates it. Every number shows its derivation; a live dimensioned floor plan, a detailed live 3D view (three.js: instanced uprights, beams and pallets, a travel-time heat map of every position, click a slot for its route and cycle time) and the FreeCAD reference model all come from the same parameters. Metric or imperial. Fully available in English and Latin American Spanish, with Spanish column names recognised in imported data.

title: Tube Flow
description: A validated 3D lattice-Boltzmann flow lab on the GPU: spheres, STL shapes and NACA wing sections in a tube, in real fluids and units. The D3Q19 solver uses TRT/regularised collision, curved-wall interpolated bounce-back and mass-conserving inlet/outlet conditions, runs in a Web Worker, and is tested against Hagen–Poiseuille pipe flow, the Haberman–Sayre wall-corrected Stokes drag and a momentum balance. Pick a fluid, tube, sphere and speed (pipe flow or a moving sphere): it reports the Reynolds number, live drag and lift coefficients, Strouhal number, pressure drop and recirculation length, says when a case needs more resolution than the grid has, labels the regime from what it measures, and exports the time series as CSV. With WebGPU it runs the same scheme on the GPU (parity-tested against the CPU solver) on grids of over a million cells, resolving the wake's symmetry-breaking and vortex shedding — benchmarked against Johnson & Patel's sphere results (wake length, side force, Strouhal number). See it with dye released from a rake or the body, Q-criterion vortex surfaces, streamlines, tracers, time-averaged slices and a movable cross-section, and record it as video. An experiment workbench swaps the sphere for an ellipsoid, cylinder, disc, cube, a bar across the tube, a wing section (NACA airfoil, symmetric or cambered, at any angle of attack, wall to wall or of finite span — with C_L, L/D, thin-airfoil comparison, angle-of-attack sweeps for the lift curve, a side-on view of the profile, slices of speed, vorticity and pressure in the profile plane, and the surface pressure distribution C_p along the chord) or your own STL shape (tested cell for cell and against the exact sphere's Stokes drag), drives it with developed, uniform or pulsatile inflow at a chosen Womersley number, runs Reynolds sweeps plotted against Schiller–Naumann and the wall-corrected Stokes drag, saves and compares runs, and exports CSV, JSON and VTK for ParaView. Five guided labs (Stokes' law and the walls, the wake bubble, shape and drag, vortex shedding, pulsatile flow and the Womersley number) walk through classic experiments step by step, and a validation report — re-runnable in the browser — shows every check the solver passes, including a grid-convergence study (observed order of accuracy, Richardson extrapolation, GCI) and GPU/CPU parity.

title: Cobot Lab
description: A browser simulator of the Universal Robots e-Series cobots — UR3e, UR5e, UR10e and UR16e, each from its published Denavit–Hartenberg and dynamics parameters — or any 6-joint arm imported from a URDF file (numerical inverse kinematics, masses from the file) — built on pure, unit-tested cores. Kinematics: forward and analytic inverse kinematics (all 8 solutions), Jacobian and a manipulability 'dexterity' meter. Motion: MoveJ with synchronised trapezoidal joint profiles, MoveL straight-line and MoveC circular tool paths solved by IK at every step and retimed to stay inside every joint's speed limit. Drag a target handle and the arm follows it live, or plan the target and send the arm with Move J / Move L; cycle through the alternative arm configurations that reach the same tool pose. A collision guard refuses anything that would hit the table or the arm itself. Live joint position/speed/acceleration plots, tool pose telemetry and a tip trace. Physics runs on Rapier (WebAssembly) with the arm itself solid, so its links and fingers push blocks around; a real pick & place reads the workpiece's pose from the simulation, lines the grasp up with it, carries it on a fixed joint and releases it. Drop obstacles on the table and a collision-free path planner (RRT-Connect with shortcutting) routes Move J and pick & place around them. Motor-load bars show each joint's holding torque from the published UR5e masses against its rating, and teaching overlays show the joint frames, a live DH table, the reachable workspace and the dexterity ellipsoid. A teach-pendant program editor (Move J / Move L waypoints with gripper actions, run or loop) exports JSON or URScript for a real UR controller, and a share link reopens the same robot, pose, program and obstacles. A ROS bridge (rosbridge JSON protocol, ROS 1 or 2) publishes /joint_states and the tool pose and can follow joint commands, so the sim can mirror or be driven by ROS. Rendered with three.js r186: image-based studio lighting, PBR Neutral tone mapping and ambient occlusion. A guided in-app tutorial at three levels (Basic, Intermediate, Advanced) walks through every feature with highlighted controls, tasks that tick off as you do them and a 'Do it for me' button, or reads as a written guide. Vendored three.js + Rapier.

title: Chess
description: Play chess against a friend on one screen, or against the open-source Stockfish 18 engine (WebAssembly, runs in your browser) at eight strength levels from beginner to full strength — full rules including castling, en passant, promotion with a piece picker, checkmate, stalemate and every draw rule (threefold repetition, the 50-move rule, insufficient material), all from one perft-verified rules module. After every game an automatic review grades each move by how much it lowered the mover's winning chances (inaccuracy, mistake, blunder; book moves from the CC0 Lichess opening catalogue), plots the evaluation, scores each side's accuracy and lets you retry your mistakes until you find the better move, with a second Stockfish worker so analysis never disturbs the opponent. Step through any game, analyse any position (three engine lines, the online endgame tablebase for seven pieces or fewer, opening names and book moves). Resign and draw offers (Stockfish judges an offer by evaluating the position), clocks with increment from bullet to classical, moves typed in algebraic notation, PGN and FEN import and export, and links that replay a game move by move. Click a piece to see its legal destinations dotted in (rings mark captures), watch moves slide into place, flip the board to face the other player, undo, and follow the algebraic move log with a live captured-material count. Five board colourways, remembered between visits, and a 3D view you can tilt and turn by dragging — the pieces stand up and face you, and everything still works. A Staunton piece option swaps in the classic Cburnett SVG set in 2D and, in 3D, real lathe-modelled pieces rendered with three.js (WebGL) with lighting and shadows. Ported from a Python/Tkinter original (included in the folder). Includes a chess course in eight levels: beginner to advanced, then opening courses (eight openings, each drilled move by move against the Lichess opening catalogue), middlegame plans tested on real Lichess puzzles, and endgames played out against perfect defence from the Lichess tablebase, where a move that throws the win away is taken back with the reason. That makes 54 lessons with exercises on the board (every solution checked by the rules engine, the tactics against Stockfish), in English, Spanish, Afrikaans, German, Danish and Dutch, any other language through on-device or web translation, and optional spoken instructions; every move exercise can be played out against Stockfish in one click. A puzzle trainer adds 44,943 puzzles from the public-domain Lichess database (balanced across ratings 400–3000, all 73 themes, each replayed through the rules engine when built), a personal Glicko-2 puzzle rating, theme practice linked from each course lesson, a daily puzzle, timed runs and per-theme success rates. A personal learning layer ties it together. A coach against Stockfish checks each move before it is played and names the tactic it would allow ("Qh5 is a blunder: it allows a loose piece"), offers hints and a threat view, and steps back as you need it less. Reviewed games are labelled by the tactic each mistake allowed or missed (a recogniser tuned against 11,000 labelled Lichess puzzles). Missed puzzles and your own game mistakes return by spaced repetition (1, 3, 7, 16 and 35 days), and a My training page shows strengths and weaknesses by theme and builds a weekly plan from them. A kids' mode (Chess for kids) teaches young children the pieces in eight worlds of star-collecting, capture and checkmate levels. Every level's three-star target is the proven fewest moves, found by search. A pawn war against a gentle computer, a mascot knight who reads every instruction aloud in six languages, stars, trophies, and big squares for small fingers complete it. Children can also play whole games against three gentle computer opponents. Sir Hop narrates each move, asks before a piece is left where it can be taken, warns when one is attacked, and awards medals.

title: Problem Log (Android)
description: A native Android app that turns a spoken or typed problem description into a structured record — title, summary, category, short-term mitigation, long-term solution — via a forced tool-call to Claude, with every generated field editable before you save it. Records live in an on-device SQLite database; the only network call is your phone talking straight to the Anthropic API with your own key, held in the Android Keystore. No backend, no account. Built with Flutter — bring your own API key to run it.

title: Othello (Android)
description: A native Android port of the Othello sub-app below — the same rules engine and negamax AI (four strengths, full endgame solve), rebuilt from JavaScript to Dart with a CustomPainter board renderer. Play the computer or pass-and-play on a 6×6, 8×8 or 10×10 board, with the same disc colourways and board felts as the web version, undo, move log, and a Material 3 light/dark theme. Built with Flutter.

title: Go
description: Play Go (Baduk / Weiqi) against the computer or a friend on one screen. Full rules — group capture, liberties, suicide prevention and the ko rule — with a ghost stone on hover and a ring on the last move. Choose a 9×9, 13×13 or 19×19 board with proper star points, set the komi, and pick from five goban woods. Two passes open a scoring phase: click any group to mark it dead, then the game is settled by area — stones plus surrounded territory plus komi. Undo, move log, capture counts and a heuristic computer opponent at three strengths. Single file, no dependencies.

title: Othello
description: Play Othello (Reversi) against the computer or a friend on one screen. Legal moves are dotted in, captures flip with a 3D animation, and the last move is ringed. Four computer strengths run a negamax search with alpha-beta pruning, a positional weight table, mobility and corner heuristics, and a full endgame solve. Choose a 6×6, 8×8 or 10×10 board — the AI rebuilds its positional map and search depth to match — plus six disc colourways and six board surfaces, remembered between visits. Undo, move log, passes and game-over detection all handled. A "How the code is built" section walks through the architecture and shows the page's own source. Single file, no dependencies.

title: Real Options for Network Design
description: Prices the flexibility in a supply network design against a fair baseline: commit now, the best fixed design, wait and see, stage and expand, and a lease with break clauses, each with its optimal policy on a binomial demand lattice; every owned site can also be sold, or mothballed and restarted, and the staged site can sell capacity back in steps. A network page values two correlated regions: a central hub that pools demand, two regional hubs, a pilot hub with a cheaper option on the second (a compound option), or waiting, with a 2D decision map and a correlation sweep. Calibrate volatility and growth from your own demand history, compare scenarios, print a decision report, and learn it with a beginner, intermediate and advanced tutorial illustrated with diagrams of every strategy and concept. Fully available in English and Latin American Spanish. A decision window separate from the asset life, build and expansion lead times, a 3PL that covers unmet demand up to a limit, a market ceiling, and a WACC or risk-neutral basis. A decision map of build and expansion triggers, payoff and NPV distributions over simulated paths, value against volatility, a sensitivity tornado, the equations, and shareable scenario links. 181 automated tests, including convergence to Black–Scholes and an exact reduction from the network to the single site.

title: Network Design Visuals
description: A browsable library of 17 supply-chain network-design visualizations, ordered simple → advanced: demand bars, cost-to-serve stacks, O–D flow maps, an echelon Sankey, lane-cost matrices, Pareto and tornado charts, a capacitated network graph, service-coverage rings, a cost–service efficient frontier, and strategic views — center-of-gravity / greenfield k-means, capacity-constrained catchment maps, animated throughput, phased network evolution, and a capacity-aware disruption-impact matrix (fails each DC in turn, re-sources its markets to whichever surviving site has room, and flags the ones that don't). Every example runs on one shared synthetic network. Single file, no dependencies.

title: Cube Studio
description: A 3×3 cube in 3D and as a 2D net: scramble it from a truly random position and watch a short Kociemba two-phase solution play out move by move. Solutions are checked by an independent cube model; 1,000-position test suite.

title: Scientific Calculator
description: A keyboard-friendly scientific calculator with a real recursive-descent expression parser (no eval), DEG/RAD/GRAD modes, memory, inverse trig via a 2nd key, and a running calculation tape. A FIN strip adds financial functions — present/future value, payment, rate and number-of-periods solvers, NPV, IRR, straight-line depreciation, and simple/compound interest. Single file, no dependencies.

title: Snake
description: A classic grid-based Snake game built with Python's Tkinter — pause/resume, increasing speed, and a game-over overlay. No external dependencies.
